payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Stuffing the paper into the cup
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Paper is stuffed into the cup.
node.criteria: Return yes when support 1 passes: the requested outcome is visibly complete. Return no only when support 1 fails and support 2 fails, establishing that no requested change has progressed. Return partial when support 1 fails and support 2 passes, establishing some progress without completion. Return unknown whenever the evidence needed to distinguish these alternatives is unresolved. A skipped support is unobserved, not automatically inapplicable; on any skipped path, return a decision only if the remaining evidence establishes that same outcome under the rubric, otherwise return unknown. Supporting evidence earns no completion credit independently, and unrelated edits do not count as progress.
node.binding: Target: The paper is visibly placed inside the cup, with evidence that it has been stuffed into it rather than merely resting nearby or on its rim.. Reference: The requested edit is stated in the instruction: “Stuffing the paper into the cup”..

node_traces.evidence: Both supporting checks are unresolved: neither establishes that the paper is stuffed into the cup nor whether any progress toward that outcome occurred.

dependencies.evidence: The source shows a white paper-like item and a blue cup, but the edited image shows a blue printed item and a reddish object. There is not enough visual evidence to identify these as the same paper and cup from the source or establish that the paper was stuffed inside the cup.

The source shows a white paper and a blue cup, but the edited image shows a hand holding a blue printed item near a reddish object. The source paper and cup cannot be reliably identified in the edited image, so progress toward stuffing the paper into the cup cannot be established.

response.content: {"text":"The node’s outcome logic is appropriately conservative, but its evidence binding is too brittle: it treats the edited objects as unidentifiable rather than assessing whether the blue printed item could be the source paper and whether the reddish object could be the cup. Improve the supporting checks to compare source and edited objects using visible shape, material, color, and scene context while allowing appearance changes; separately assess completion (paper visibly inside the cup) and partial progress (a plausible attempt to insert the same paper into the same cup). Here, the edit shows a hand holding a blue printed item against or near a reddish rounded object, with no clear evidence that the paper is inside a cup or that either object matches the source. That supports no progress only if the checks can establish the objects and rule out relevant progress; otherwise retain unknown. Do not convert high confidence in unresolved identity into negative evidence. Keep the existing distinction between complete, partial, no progress, and unresolved, and investigate whether the checks’ identity-matching criterion is causing valid visual evidence to be discarded. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is indicated."}
